name: Where the money comes from
reg: Primary vs. secondary market · the GSEs

items.text: When a bank hands over a few hundred thousand dollars, that money isn't sitting in a vault waiting for you. There's a much larger machine behind the loan, and it decides who gets funded and on what terms. It has two halves. The primary market is where loans are made — the lenders and brokers who take the application and write the mortgage. The secondary market is where those finished loans get bought and sold afterward, as investments.

A lender only has so much cash, and a thirty-year loan ties up three hundred thousand dollars of it for decades — unless the lender can sell the loan and get the money back now. So that's exactly what it does. A lender originates the loan, sells it into the secondary market, takes the fresh cash, and lends it again to the next borrower. The loan you signed may change hands within weeks of closing. None of your terms change when it does.

The biggest buyers are two government-sponsored enterprises — private companies operating under a federal charter. Fannie Mae, the Federal National Mortgage Association, and Freddie Mac, the Federal Home Loan Mortgage Corporation. Both buy conventional loans from lenders. Once they own a pile of loans they bundle them into a mortgage-backed security — an investment that pools many mortgages and sells shares of the monthly payments to investors around the world. Fannie is the older of the two. It dates to nineteen thirty-eight, and it was created for exactly this problem. Then there's a third player, Ginnie Mae, the Government National Mortgage Association, and Ginnie is different in two ways. It's an actual government agency, not a chartered private company. And it doesn't buy loans at all. Instead it guarantees the securities built from F-H-A, V-A, and U-S-D-A loans. Buys versus guarantees. That's the distinction the exam is after.

A lender will only write a loan it can sell, and Fannie or Freddie will only buy a loan that meets their rules. A loan that fits those rules — including a maximum amount they'll purchase — is a conforming loan. Which is the real answer to a question every new originator asks eventually: why are the underwriting guidelines the way they are? Because somebody downstream has to be willing to buy this loan, so it has to be built to their standard from the very start. The guidelines aren't the lender's preferences. They're the buyer's terms. And selling the loan doesn't mean the lender walks away — lenders usually keep the servicing, collecting the payment and managing escrow, earning a steady fee long after the loan itself belongs to somebody else.
